title: Colombia Update — Aug 10, 2026
summary: Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as Colombia's president on August 7 at Arena USC in Cali — the first inauguration held outside Bogotá — alongside VP José Manuel Restrepo, pledging to abandon Petro's Total Peace policy for a military offensive against armed groups backed by a new US 'Plan Patriota 2.0' security partnership. Gustavo Petro left office still alleging election fraud, having warned days earlier that the transition could spark 'civil war,' closed his foreign agenda with a symbolic final trip to Cuba, and skipped the ceremony (which the Historic Pact bloc boycotted) for an AI-generated farewell video. Security proved the central story of the handover: police intercepted a bus loaded with nearly half a ton of explosives near Cali just before the inauguration, and a car bomb hit a Cauca toll plaza the day after, both blamed on FARC dissident factions. Separately, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake near San José del Palmar, Chocó killed at least 20 people on August 10 and caused serious damage in Quibdó, Pereira, and Manizales.

title: Colombia Update — Jul 16, 2026
summary: President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won Colombia's June 21 runoff by the narrowest margin in the country's history — 49.66% to Iván Cepeda's 48.70%, about 250,000 votes — becoming the most-voted candidate ever. Outgoing President Petro refused to recognize the result, alleging fraud and foreign (Israeli/US) interference; the EU, OAS, and Carter Center observer missions all found no irregularities, and Petro's own Attorney General dismissed the claims. The dispute briefly halted the presidential transition on July 7 before cabinet formation resumed, with de la Espriella naming ministers for Transportation, Justice, Commerce, Housing, Sports, and Foreign Affairs (career diplomat Omar Bula Escobar). On July 14 he announced elimination of 229 government posts, including the Office of the High Commissioner for Peace that runs Petro's Total Peace negotiations. Separately, the Colombian peso rallied to a six-year high (~3,252/USD) on the election outcome.

title: Colombia Update — May 27, 2026
summary: Four days from the May 31 presidential vote, Colombia's campaign concluded as the most violent in decades: 61 political leaders killed, 139 municipalities at extreme electoral risk (MOE), journalist attacks up 175% versus the 2022 cycle, and the U.S. warning it may not recognize results if armed group interference is proven. Front-runner Iván Cepeda (left, ~44%) faces right-wing challengers Paloma Valencia and Abelardo de la Espriella; no first-round winner is expected, with a June runoff near-certain. The Banco de la República raised its policy rate to 11.25% in two 2026 hikes as inflation re-accelerated, adding economic pressure to the post-election transition. A new contested-claims entry captures the debate over whether the U.S. recognition threat was legitimate election monitoring or improper sovereignty interference.
